{{Short description|Optimization method}}
The '''Davidon–Fletcher–Powell formula''' (or '''DFP'''; named after [[William C. Davidon]], [[Roger Fletcher (mathematician)|Roger Fletcher]], and [[Michael J. D. Powell]]) finds the solution to the secant equation that is closest to the current estimate and satisfies the curvature condition. It was the first [[quasi-Newton method]] to generalize the [[secant method]] to a multidimensional problem. This update maintains the symmetry and positive definiteness of the [[Hessian matrix]].

Given a [[smoothness|smooth]] function <math>f(x)</math>, its [[gradient]] (<math>\nabla f</math>), and [[positive-definite matrix|positive-definite]] [[Hessian matrix]] <math>B</math>, the [[Taylor series]] is

:<math>f(x_k+s_k) = f(x_k) + \nabla f(x_k)^T s_k + \frac{1}{2} s^T_k {B} s_k + \dots,</math>

and the [[Taylor series]] of the gradient itself (secant equation)

:<math>\nabla f(x_k+s_k) = \nabla f(x_k) + B s_k + \dots</math>

is used to update <math>B</math>.  

The DFP formula finds a solution that is symmetric, positive-definite and closest to the current approximate value of <math>B_k</math>:

:<math>B_{k+1}=
(I - \gamma_k y_k s_k^T) B_k (I - \gamma_k s_k y_k^T) + \gamma_k y_k y_k^T,</math>

where

:<math>y_k = \nabla f(x_k+s_k) - \nabla f(x_k),</math>
:<math>\gamma_k = \frac{1}{y_k^T s_k},</math>

and <math>B_k</math> is a symmetric and [[positive-definite matrix]].

The corresponding update to the inverse Hessian approximation <math>H_k = B_k^{-1}</math> is given by

:<math>H_{k+1} = H_k - \frac{H_k y_k y_k^T H_k}{y_k^T H_k y_k} + \frac{s_k s_k^T}{y_k^{T} s_k}.</math>

<math>B</math> is assumed to be positive-definite, and the vectors <math>s_k^T</math> and <math>y</math> must satisfy the curvature condition

: <math>s_k^T y_k = s_k^T B s_k > 0.</math>

The DFP formula is quite effective, but it was soon superseded by the [[Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno algorithm|Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno formula]], which is its [[Duality (mathematics)|dual]] (interchanging the roles of ''y'' and ''s'').<ref>{{cite book |first=Mordecai |last=Avriel |title=Nonlinear Programming: Analysis and Methods |publisher=Prentice-Hall |year=1976 |isbn=0-13-623603-0 |pages=352–353 }}</ref>

== Compact representation ==
By unwinding the matrix recurrence for <math>B_k </math>, the DFP formula can be expressed
as a [[Compact quasi-Newton representation|compact matrix representation]]. Specifically, defining

<math display="block"> S_k = \begin{bmatrix} s_0 & s_1 & \ldots & s_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>
<math display="block"> Y_k = \begin{bmatrix} y_0 & y_1 & \ldots & y_{k-1} \end{bmatrix}, </math>

and upper triangular and diagonal matrices

<math display="block"> \big(R_k\big)_{ij} := \big(R^{\text{SY}}_k\big)_{ij} = s^T_{i-1}y_{j-1}, \quad \big(R^{\text{YS}}_k\big)_{ij} = y^T_{i-1}s_{j-1}, \quad 
(D_k)_{ii} := \big(D^{\text{SY}}_k\big)_{ii} = s^T_{i-1}y_{i-1} \quad \quad \text{ for } 1 \le i \le j \le k  </math>

the DFP matrix has the equivalent formula

<math display="block"> B_k = B_0 + J_k N^{-1}_k J^T_k, </math>

<math display="block"> J_k = \begin{bmatrix} Y_k & Y_k - B_0 S_k \end{bmatrix} </math>

<math display="block"> N_k = 
\begin{bmatrix} 0_{k \times k} & R^{\text{YS}}_k \\ 
\big( R^{\text{YS}}_k \big)^T & R_k+R^T_k-(D_k+S^T_k B_0 S_k) 
\end{bmatrix} </math>

The inverse compact representation can be found by applying the [[Woodbury matrix identity|Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury inverse]] to <math>B_k</math>. The compact representation is particularly useful for limited-memory and constrained problems.<ref name="brust24">{{cite arXiv |eprint=2403.12206 |class=math.OC |first1=J. J. |last1=Brust |title=Useful Compact Representations for Data-Fitting |year=2024}}</ref>
